event.title: An Artist’s America: Toward a More Perfect Union
event.description:
"An Artist’s America" will be on view at Haas Arts Library from June 8 through Nov. 8.

 

Artists have a long history of documenting, interrogating, and resisting American political administrations. The works in this exhibit comment on the radical roots of America and its complex history through artist books. Featured artists highlight socio-cultural, environmental, and socio-economic observations and experiences of American people.

 

2026 marks the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, and this founding document established a radical contrary to the British Crown with the key statement “all men are created equal”, which marked the beginning of a nation-state centered on freedom, self-determination, and unalienable rights. In some artist books shared here, the concept of the “American Dream” is interrogated with an exploration of the realities of governmental policy and its legacy. In others, artists document local communities to initiate conversations about America as simultaneously independent and culturally interdependent. Other themes explored are historic events and figures, democracy, public policy, citizenship, restorative justice, and border relations.

 

Curator: De’Ivyion "Ivy" Drew, 2025-2026 Kress Fellow in Art Librarianship, Yale University.

 

Please join us for a curator’s tour celebrating the opening of the exhibition “An Artist’s America: Toward a More Perfect Union” on Tuesday, June 9th from 3:30pm to 5:00pm in Haas Arts Library. Remarks will begin at 3:45pm.

event.title: Poetry and the Everyday   Virtual Gallery
event.ticket_cost: Free and open to the public
event.description:
Online exhibition

An exercise in seeing the poetry that exists all around us... 

 

This gallery features a collection of art created by students that responds to the questions: Through any medium of your choice, consider the ways you interact with poetry on a daily basis, if at all. For example, can poetry be found in nature? Are our conversations with one another in some way, poetic? Can poetry still truly influence societal change, in our contemporary moment, or is it primarily an isolated art form? 

 

Explore the reflections and creative insights of Yale undergraduate and graduate students from different programs through their artworks presented in a variety of media and formats. 

 

Curated by Babette Thomas '26 GRD 

 

Leaf on Grids

by Nuria Sanchez Matias '30 GRD
 

The Way We Say Goodbye

by Xinning Shao '26

 

Conversations with Ancestors

by Inkpa Mani-Lara Ruiz '26 ART

Akwaaba.

On Writing Nothing

by Makda Assefa '26

 

The Hillhouse Oak Trees

event.title: RUSUNUNGUKO (liberty / independence / freedom)
event.description:
Free and open to the public during building hours. 

Please check HERE for most up to date hours, and closures. 

Designer and visual artist Nontsikelelo Mutiti is the assistant professor and director of graduate studies in graphic design at the Yale School of Art. Mutiti’s printed works, films, and installations engage with the history and aesthetics of hair braiding in black life. “Ruka” (Shona for “to weave, braid, or knit”) brings social binding alongside physical braiding; the arrangements of salons, living rooms, and porches where hair is braided provide social contexts for her projects. Witness Mutiti's latest work, RUSUNUNGUKO (liberty / independence / freedom) in The Dome Gallery on the upper level at Yale Schwarzman Center during the building's open hours.

Extended through 2027!
